intro: Liszt’s pupil Eugen d’Albert plays Chopin’s Butterfly étude on an Odeon recording from 1912–13. Its short slurs and detached octaves keep the piano hopping between phrases.

sections.label: A · Short slurs and detached octaves
sections.mNote: The right hand alternates connected pairs with clipped notes

sections.label: B · Octaves hop across the keyboard
sections.mNote: The little four-note figure changes key and climbs

sections.label: C · The short figure returns
sections.mNote: Right-hand octaves continue above the left hand’s leaps

sections.label: D · The last piano chords fade
sections.mNote: The study closes and the piano falls silent

cues.title: A small, springing figure
cues.text: The right hand’s four-note groups mix short slurs with detached notes and octaves. The left hand leaps between bass notes and chords. Chopin carries this little figure through the whole étude, changing its key and height on the keyboard.
cues.evidence: The recurring motif, key changes and staccato octaves: Mieczysław Tomaszewski, https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/263. Left-hand leaps and right-hand groups: Fred Yu, https://www.ourchopin.com/analysis/etude25.html.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: From Glasgow to Liszt
cues.text: D’Albert grows up far from the German concert halls that make his name. Born in Glasgow in 1864, he studies in London with teachers including Arthur Sullivan, then goes to Liszt. Alongside his career at the piano, he writes operas; Tiefland reaches the stage in 1903.
cues.evidence: Baker’s Biographical Dictionary of Musicians: Glasgow birth, London training with Sullivan, study with Liszt and the 15 November 1903 Prague premiere of Tiefland. https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/dalbert-eugen-actually-eugene-francischarles

cues.title: Two études on one side
cues.text: Odeon pairs Butterfly with Chopin’s F-minor étude, Op. 25 No. 2, on catalogue number 76563. Both pieces share one recording matrix. This short G♭-major study is the second half of that original disc side.
cues.evidence: Printed Symposium 1146 track list gives both études the same Odeon catalogue number 76563 and matrix xxB 5731, dated 1912/3. https://archive.org/download/02-eugen-d-albert-syposium-1146/D%27Albert%20tracks.jpg. The Archive filename specifies March 1913; the printed discography gives only the year range.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
